# Arcade

> Arcade is the enterprise-ready actions runtime for AI agents.

Arcade is the enterprise-ready actions runtime for AI agents. We enforce your security policies on every action, execute reliably across any system, and govern agents centrally in production. Configure once and use any model, framework, and client — deploy the first agent the same way you deploy the hundredth.

Arcade delivers three capabilities. Enforce (Agent Authorization): deploy agents your security team approves — Arcade handles OAuth and manages user tokens, API keys, and secrets, then enforces your existing IdP, DLP, SIEM, and compliance policies plus per-action authorization at runtime. Execute (Agent-Optimized Tools): the largest catalog of agent-optimized tools — 7,500+ across 81 MCP servers, built for reliable execution at scale, not thin API wrappers. Govern (Agent Lifecycle Governance): a central control plane with a shared registry, version control, visibility filtering, and OpenTelemetry audit logs.

## Who this is for

Arcade docs serve two audiences. Start with the path that matches your goal:

- To build agents and tools (call tools, create MCP servers, ship user-facing agents), go to Build: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build. New to Arcade? Start with the agent quickstart: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/quickstarts/call-tool-agent.
- To deploy, secure, and govern Arcade for an organization (hosting, identity, gateways, audit logs), go to Operate: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate. New to operating Arcade? Start with the operator quickstart: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/quickstart.

## Getting Started

- [Home](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/home): The "Arcade Docs" page provides guides, resources, sample agents, and references specifically for Arcade authentication providers and MCP servers, aimed at assisting agents and developers in effectively utilizing these technologies.

- [Add metadata to your tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/add-tool-metadata): This documentation teaches you how to add structured metadata annotations to MCP tools using `ToolMetadata`, which helps MCP clients, policy engines, and tool-selection systems understand what each tool does and how it behaves. You'll learn about the three axes of metadata (classification, behavior, and extras), how to classify tools by their target service domain, and how behavior flags map to MCP annotations like `readOnlyHint` and `destructiveHint`.

It covers how auth providers work during execution, provides step-by-step instructions for implementing authorization, and explains both built-in providers (Reddit, Slack, Google, GitHub) and custom OAuth2 implementations.
- [Adding Resource Server Auth to Your MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/secure-your-server/secure-your-mcp-server): This documentation page teaches you how to secure an HTTP MCP server using OAuth 2.1 Resource Server authentication, enabling tool-level authorization and secrets for self-hosted deployments. It explains what Resource Server auth is, why it's needed to protect HTTP MCP servers, and provides guidance on configuring your server to validate Bearer tokens and support multiple authorization servers.

It details how Arcade stores and manages different categories of data—including user-controlled application data, platform-controlled monitoring data, and training data for ML/AI models—along with user controls for data retention, deletion, and opt-out options for training consent.

After authentication with an Arcade account, users can describe what integrations they need (like Gmail and Google Calendar) and the AI will automatically select appropriate tools and create a gateway, which can then be added back to their chat client for use.

It covers transport-specific configuration options, secret management, and customization parameters for popular clients including Cursor IDE, VS Code, and Claude Desktop.

- [Capture mode](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/evaluate-tools/capture-mode): Capture mode records tool calls from models without evaluating them, allowing you to bootstrap test expectations and debug model behavior. You can run it with the `--capture` flag on any evaluation command, review the captured JSON output, and then convert those calls into formal test expectations. It supports multiple runs, conversation context, different formats, and multiple model providers for comprehensive testing and comparison.
- [Checking Tool Authorization Status](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling/custom-apps/check-auth-status): This guide teaches you how to check whether tools have the necessary authorization and permissions before executing them, which is useful for displaying authorization requirements in your UI and pre-checking tool availability. It provides step-by-step instructions for registering an OAuth application in Clerk, configuring the necessary scopes and settings, and copying the required credentials (Client Secret, Client ID, and Discovery URL) into Arcade's User Source form.

The documentation explains how to set up tracks, register tools for each track, create test cases with track-specific expectations, and run evaluations that show per-track performance scores. It also covers advanced features like mixing regular and comparative cases, using capture mode with tracks, and running multi-model comparative evaluations.

This allows you to enforce access policies, compliance rules, and data transformations without modifying your existing tools or agents.

- [Rate Limiting](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/contextual-access/rate-limiting): Rate limiting in Arcade allows platform operators to cap how often tools can be called by defining rules that specify which tools to limit, maximum call counts, and time windows—these limits are enforced natively by the Arcade Engine before each tool execution without requiring a separate webhook server. Rate limits protect upstream services from runaway agents, keep workloads within vendor quotas, and can be configured through the Dashboard or API with support for exact tool matches, toolkit-wide rules, or global limits across all tools.
- [Remote MCP servers](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers): This documentation page explains how to register and use remote MCP servers—servers hosted outside of Arcade by your team, a vendor, or a partner—so their tools become available across your entire project scope. This is useful when a tool call fails due to invalid parameters and you want to give the model guidance to generate better parameters on the next attempt, such as providing a list of valid options when a user lookup fails.

It explains Arcade's error hierarchy system and shows users how to debug failed tool calls using Arcade's recorded execution history.
- [Tool executions](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/tool-executions): Arcade records every tool execution in a project, capturing which tool ran, for which user, when, and its outcome, with inputs and outputs restricted to project admins for security. This page helps developers debug failed tool runs by reviewing exact inputs and outputs, and helps platform operators monitor tool usage and ensure compliance across their projects.
- [Tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/resources/tools): This documentation page provides an overview of Arcade's ecosystem for AI tools, enabling users to explore a catalog of pre-built integrations, create custom tools, and contribute their own tools to the community. It outlines the benefits of using Arcade tools, such as built
- [Types of Tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/improve/types-of-tools): Arcade offers two types of tools—Optimized and Unoptimized—that differ in their design approach but work identically through the same interface. Optimized tools are carefully designed to match AI chat interfaces and improve reliability by handling complex workflows automatically, while Unoptimized tools mirror original HTTP endpoints and require more careful evaluation before production use. Both types can be used seamlessly together in Arcade's Dashboard and SDK clients.
- [Understanding `Context` and tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/runtime-data-access): The `Context` class provides tools with access to both runtime capabilities and tool-specific data, such as OAuth tokens, secrets, and user information, as well as features like logging, LLM sampling, user elicitation, and progress reporting. This guide explains how to use the `Context` object that is automatically passed to tools by the MCP server to securely access authentication credentials and leverage runtime features during tool execution.

- [Use Arcade in GitHub Copilot](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/github-copilot): This documentation page guides users through connecting GitHub Copilot to an Arcade MCP Gateway, enabling AI-assisted development with access to custom tools across multiple IDEs including VS Code, JetBrains, Visual Studio, Eclipse, and XCode. - [Use Arcade in Visual Studio Code](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/visual-studio-code): This documentation page provides a step-by-step guide for connecting Visual Studio Code to an Arcade MCP Gateway, enabling users to set up and run their MCP server within the IDE. - [User Sources](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity/user-sources): A User Source connects an MCP Gateway to your OIDC identity provider, allowing end users to sign in with their existing identities instead of requiring Arcade to manage them separately. This documentation guides you through registering an OAuth client with your identity provider and creating a User Source in Arcade to enable production authentication for your gateways.
- [User-facing agents](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/user-facing-agents): This documentation guides agent developers on building and deploying agents that operate on behalf of end users with proper authorization and authentication. It provides resources for implementing secure authentication in production environments and integrating user authorization into tool-calling workflows.
- [What are tools?](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling): This documentation page explains what tools are in the context of language models and how Arcade enables tool calling—the ability for AI models to interact with external systems and APIs to accomplish tasks beyond text generation. It covers the use cases for tool calling, how it works, the authorization challenges Arcade solves, and introduces Tool Augmented Generation (TAG) as a flexible alternative to retrieval-based approaches.
- [Why evaluate tools?](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/evaluate-tools/why-evaluate): Tool evaluations ensure AI models use your tools correctly in production by measuring whether the model selects the right tools and provides accurate parameters before deployment. Without evaluation, models risk misinterpreting user intents, providing incorrect arguments, or skipping necessary tool calls, which Arcade's evaluation framework helps prevent by comparing actual tool calls against expected ones and scoring them based on tool selection and parameter accuracy.
- [Windows environment setup](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/setup/windows-environment): This documentation page provides step-by-step instructions for setting up the Arcade CLI on Windows, emphasizing the use of the `uv` package manager while offering fallback options with `pip`. It includes prerequisites, installation methods, validation steps, and troubleshooting tips to ensure
